question: The trade agreement between the EU and Indonesia, particularly the arrangements for tuna fillets, is raising concerns in the European fisheries sector and has recently been drawing extensive media attention from outlets such as La Voz de Galicia1 and ABC2.

The agreement fully liberalises tuna fillets, treating them differently from other tuna products, such as tuna loins and canned tuna, which are fortunately still subject to tariff quotas. Fillets are a high value-added segment for the EU fleet, which has also invested heavily to position itself in this niche market and to meet the high health requirements.
Given that Indonesia is one of the world’s leading tuna producers: 1.
Has the Commission carried out a specific assessment of the economic impact that could be had on the EU’s tuna fleet due to tariffs on tuna fillets being completely eliminated?

Since it is expected that tuna fillet imports will increase and since they are destined primarily for direct consumption, does the Commission consider the guarantees offered by the standards Indonesian operators are required to meet to be equivalent to those provided by the standards applicable to EU operators, particularly with regard to health and food safety?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) Trade in frozen tuna fillets has been fully liberalised, and as of entry into force, in most free trade agreements concluded by the EU to date. No particular concern has been flagged to the Commission in this respect.

Throughout the negotiations for the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement1 (CEPA) with Indonesia, the Commission engaged regularly with stakeholders to identify key interests and sensitivities. It carried out a Sustainability Impact Assessment, looking at potential economic impacts of the agreement, and shared with the co-legislators all the EU tariff offers.

In the nine years of CEPA negotiations, the Commission did not receive any indication that a liberalisation of frozen tuna fillets would be disruptive for the EU fleet or industry. The preferential treatment of products identified as sensitive under the CEPA, such as canned tuna and tuna loins, has been carefully handled in the negotiations.

The balanced outcome ensures modalities to avoid disruptions for EU industry, through strict rules of origin for all tuna products and tariff-rate quotas calibrated on current trade flows for canned tuna (800 metric tonnes) and for tuna loins (5 000 metric tonnes).

For tuna fillets, despite lack of apparent sensitivity, the Commission negotiated a seven-year staging period for the tariff elimination, which provides EU industry with an additional transition period to adjust if necessary. As regards the EU health and food safety rules, the CEPA does not affect their application.
Indonesian products placed on the EU market, including frozen tuna fillets, will continue being subject to strict EU rules and related controls.
